newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU prospects enter critical period.
newsitem.headline: EMU prospects enter critical period.

text.p: Although Germany's internal row over the Bundesbank's gold reserves appears to have been defused, Europe's planned single currency still faces an uncertain future with several formidable hurdles ahead.

Analysts say three major concerns will dominate the political landscape this month, all of which have the potential of either putting EMU on a firm footing for 1999 or causing a postponement of the project.

Foremost, with Bonn forced to back down from its plan to use the proceeds from a revaluation of gold reserves to bolster its 1997 finances, some combination of tax increases and spending cuts will have to be found quickly.
Analysts say the way in which this is achieved is open to considerable speculation, but some recourse to higher petrol taxes now appears to be a distinct possibility.
From a timing standpoint, however, a budget accord must be secured by the end of June if there is to be any hope of Bonn bringing its deficit near three percent of Gross Domestic Product.

"You definitely need an agreement before July 1. Otherwise they will not have any chance to bring this through parliament before the summer recess," said Werner Becker, economist at Deutsche Bank Research in Frankfurt.

A second worry is France. The new French government's position on the EU's stability and growth pact, an accord designed to restrain spending among countries joining EMU, has prompted uneasiness among diplomats, worried that Paris might want to alter some its key aspects.

French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has said he does not feel bound by the pact and wants it renegotiated. With the accord due to be approved by EU leaders at a summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17, there are questions over how keen the French will be to alter the terms of the agreement.

Politically, EU diplomats say they find it difficult to envisage circumstances under which the 15-nation bloc would reopen talks on the pact, which incorporates stiff fines for EMU governments with excessive deficits.
A more likely scenario sees France's concerns on jobs addressed by including an employment chapter in a revised Maastricht Treaty, a subject that will dominate the June summit.

Another worry is France's budget outlook. An audit of the government's finances is scheduled for around the middle of the month and some analysts reckon the findings will show the need for further savings.
"The new government will likely find the deficit higher than the current three percent (of GDP) official projection," said one economist at French bank in Paris.

Lastly there is the Italian question. Although events in Germany and France over the past two weeks have raised the odds of a wider group of initial EMU members -- the so-called soft euro -- there are still serious reservations in Germany over including Italy.
Speculation that Italy might refuse to sign the EU stability pact in protest has surfaced in financial markets lately, giving the Amsterdam summit yet another issue to worry about.
How financial markets manoeuvre around these potential minefields is difficult to judge, but some economists say broad trends are already beginning to emerge.
The dollar has benefited against the mark in recent days and economists at Chase Manhattan Bank in London reckon that the uptrend should continue.
A report from J.P. Morgan recommends keeping overall investment positions modest, with both sterling and dollar expected to climb further against the mark.
For the fixed-income markets, Morgan makes the following point: "Europe is not voting against EMU but it is voting against fiscal austerity, and for job creation."
As a result, investors should be selling core European government bonds.

The possibility of a softer euro, meanwhile, has improved Italy's chances of early EMU entry, making Italian bonds more attractive against both core European bonds and other peripheral markets such as Spain and Portugal.
